The phenomenologist cannot begin with a few basic propositions about human beings and then “derive” or “deduce” from them everything that can ideally be known about humanity—including everything we know about historical development—without any prior knowledge of that development.

The method of ***a priori* deduction** is found, for example, in geometry. Starting from a small number of Euclidean “axioms,” a geometer can “deduce” everything that can in general be said about geometrical figures that can be constructed with ruler and compass.

For example, without ever having “seen” a parabola, the geometer can construct one and list all its properties. This is what is meant by an ***a priori* deduction**: a deduction carried out before encountering the thing in question.
The phenomenologist proceeds in exactly the opposite direction.

Starting, say, with a parabola already given and fully formed, the phenomenologist would look for the “axioms” that must be accepted in order to determine all its properties and make it possible to construct it.

In this sense, Phenomenology can be regarded as an “axiomatics” of human existence, if we understand “axiomatics” in the sense given to the term by the great German mathematician Hilbert and his school.
Starting from humanity as it presently exists, Phenomenology searches for the basic, irreducible, and underivable premises without which this present state could not exist.
Once it has found them, it tries to deduce the present state from those premises, just as the geometer derives “theorems” from “axioms.”
The only difference is that the geometer can, in principle, begin by laying down the axioms. The phenomenologist must begin with a concrete historical situation that is already given.

In other words, Phenomenology deals with the problem that philosophy had been dealing with since Plato and that Kant very accurately defined as the search for the “conditions of possibility” of experience—or of appearance.
Starting from what is given in the experience of a historical phenomenon, the phenomenologist tries to reconstruct the chain of appearances that led to what is now given.
This is possible precisely because the appearance given to the phenomenologist is historical: it contains within itself all the appearances that preceded it.
And precisely for this reason the answer to the problem must be unambiguous. Only one concrete dialectical path can lead to the historical phenomenon that is given.
To discover the “conditions of possibility” of a given appearance is simply to understand it.
We can say that we fully understand something only when we know how it was “made”—that is, when we can reproduce it in thought.
We understand a geometrical figure or theorem only when we can “construct” it or “deduce” it from axioms.
Phenomenology similarly allows us to “construct” a given historical appearance in thought, beginning with the same “materials” and using the same “means” as the real history that actually created it.
A method that understands something by mentally reproducing its formation is called the genetic method. We can therefore say that the phenomenological method is “genetic.”
But we must be precise about what this means.
Phenomenology can reveal the “genesis”—the origin or development—only of something that already exists and is given to it independently of its knowledge of that genesis.
The genesis described by Phenomenology is therefore the description of the real development of reality itself, not merely a description of the way reality is reconstructed in or by thought.
To summarize everything we have said about phenomenological method, we can call it a method of ***a posteriori* deduction**.

It is a posteriori because Phenomenology can speak only about something that already exists independently of it. What it describes is in some sense given before Phenomenology begins to speak about it.
But it is still genuinely a deduction, because once Phenomenology knows an existing appearance, it can “deduce” or “construct” it: it can reproduce in thought its “genesis” or development.

Starting from a given historical or human appearance, Phenomenology can determine the number, order, and character of all the free decisions or actions that preceded and created it. It can then work backward until it reaches the first origins of the phenomenon—origins beyond which it cannot go, because they represent the indivisible minimum of humanity, the minimum conditions of historical existence, beyond which lies merely natural existence.

Once Phenomenology has determined these origins, it can then, in its exposition, “derive” or “deduce” the phenomenon from them. This can create the impression that Phenomenology is deducing the phenomenon without having known anything about it beforehand.

But as I have already said, the description of this phenomenological “deduction” is nothing other than the description, in phenomenological form, of the real historical process that actually produced the appearance in question.
It follows clearly from all this that the ***a posteriori* deductive** character of Phenomenology comes not from its method, but from the distinctive character of its object.
Phenomenological description can be deductive only because the object it describes is historical.

At bottom, Phenomenology describes the real historical process itself, viewed in its phenomenological aspect. Its “method” therefore consists only in selecting the material on the basis of a knowledge of the dialectical character of that process.

Phenomenological description takes the form of a “deduction” only because, within real history itself, appearances do not merely follow one another in time. Each appearance is the result of all those that came before it, and it could have resulted only from those that actually preceded it, not from some different sequence of appearances.
On this basis, we can say that the phenomenologist proceeds exactly as the author of an autobiography would. In this sense, the phenomenologist uses an “autobiographical method.”
When someone sets out to write an autobiography, they are in some sense trying to understand themselves and to make themselves understandable to others.
To do this, they describe their “genesis.”
They begin with what they are at the moment of writing and try to explain how and why they became what they are.
They know, of course, that if they simply recall their childhood and start only from those memories, they cannot “deduce” their present from them.

But because they know their present, they can select from the enormous number of childhood memories those that help them—and others—understand why they became precisely the person they became rather than someone else. In particular, they can understand why they now feel the need to write an autobiography at all.
Yet when they identify the characteristic features of their childhood, they will not feel that the path of their life had already been fixed once and for all at that time.
On the contrary, they will remember moments in adolescence and early adulthood when they freely made one important decision or another—decisions that help explain why they became the person they are.
Their present life will be defined only as the sum of all these decisions.
And conversely, to understand their present fully, they must reconstruct all those decisions in memory.
But once again, they can select and interpret those decisions correctly only by beginning with an understanding of what they are now.

A successful autobiography—that is, a convincing one—must show its author that a person born into the environment described, and who passed through all the stages of development described, could not have become, as an adult, anything other than what the author is.

Conversely, it must convince the author that, in order to become what they are, they necessarily had to pass through the stages they actually passed through and had to be born into precisely the environment into which they were born.
Yet none of this should hide the fact that the author could have become completely different if even one of their free decisions had been different from the decision actually made.
And in principle, such a different decision could have been made at any moment of conscious life.
A successful autobiography must therefore reveal clearly the “unused possibilities” of the life it describes.
As we already know, Phenomenology can in one sense be regarded as just such an autobiography.

The difference is that its author is not trying to understand himself as a “living” person in the full concreteness of his life. He is trying to understand himself simply and specifically as the author of this autobiography.

He wants to grasp and show what had to happen in him and for him so that, at this particular moment, he could write this particular Phenomenology, describing precisely what it describes and writing it in precisely the way he writes it.

He therefore writes a Phenomenology with philosophy in view. That is, he ultimately wants to understand himself fully as a concrete human being: a person conditioned by a particular historical situation—or, more exactly, by the way that historical situation is given to his consciousness through the knowledge and understanding he has of it.
In other words, he understands himself as conditioned by a situation taken as an “appearance” or “phenomenon.”
And since this “phenomenon” also conditions the way he writes his Phenomenology, the Phenomenology itself is nothing other than a genetic description of that appearance.

After all, the author of a Phenomenology is “a child of his time.” We can therefore say that the historical reality which appears to him is also what appears, in general, to the human beings of his age.
Consequently, although the Phenomenology is his autobiography, it is also the autobiography of humanity as a whole.

Through the consciousness of the author of a Phenomenology, humanity itself is, so to speak, remembering its past and trying to understand how and why it became what it is at this particular historical moment.
Yet the “conception” of the historical present given by a Phenomenology can never be completely exhaustive.

Phenomenology is, if one likes, “autobiographical” and therefore “subjective” in the sense that it does not show what humanity’s past really was. It shows only how that past appeared to humanity in the course of its history and how it appears to humanity at the historical moment in question.
Phenomenology therefore describes the historical sequence of the ways in which human beings appear to human beings—that is, to themselves.

But because these appearances appear to a human being, and therefore to the very kind of being that carries out the historical process, the sequence of appearances reproduces the sequence of historical events themselves, both chronologically and dialectically.
We can therefore say that a Phenomenology is nothing other than a description of the autobiographical aspect of the universal history of humanity.
If Phenomenology can be defined as a phenomenological autobiography, we must not forget that its main purpose is not simply, or even mainly, to describe its author philosophically.
Its purpose is to transform its author, through that very description, from a non-philosopher into a philosopher—that is, into someone capable of writing a complete philosophical system.

Phenomenology must therefore be “true” in more than the ordinary scientific sense, according to which the meaning of its descriptions must correspond exactly to the real content of the object described.

It must also be true in the strong sense, because it is the necessary premise of truth in that strong sense: of definitive, complete, and exhaustive knowledge of the most concrete reality—of “perfect” knowledge, or omniscience.
As we already know, the philosophical system in the strict sense—that is, Cosmology and Ontology—gives a complete answer to the following question:
What must the existing world, and the being underlying it, be like for it to be able to “appear” to human beings exactly as it actually does?
Since the answer must be definitive and therefore exhaustive, it necessarily presupposes complete knowledge of all appearances or phenomena.
That is precisely the kind of knowledge Phenomenology is, in principle, supposed to provide.
Phenomenological description must therefore be not only correct, but also complete.
On the one hand, Phenomenology must give a correct—that is, exact and exhaustive—description of each individual appearance.
On the other hand, it must describe in this way all appearances that exist, or more precisely, all essentially distinct types of appearance.
In other words, the content of Phenomenology must be true in the strong, philosophical sense.
The knowledge of phenomena that it provides must, as people say, be universal and necessary.

The universality of Phenomenology means that anyone capable of understanding its content must find that content convincing. Anyone who understands it must necessarily agree with what its author says and make the author’s discourse their own.
The necessity of Phenomenology means that neither its author nor anyone else can alter its content in any way.
Nothing can be added to it.
Nothing can be removed from it.
And everything said in the Phenomenology must be said exactly as it is said.
This also means that the knowledge it offers is definitive or perfect—true in the strong sense of the word.
It is true both because each individual description is correct, exact, and exhaustive, and because it describes everything that can in principle be described.
In this sense, phenomenological knowledge has a philosophical character.

And since philosophical knowledge is “perfect” knowledge or omniscience, not only because it is knowledge of everything but because it includes all true knowledge whatsoever, it follows that knowing that philosophical knowledge is true—that it is omniscience—is itself part of philosophical knowledge.
Philosophy must itself show, to itself and to others, that its descriptions are “universal and necessary”—that is, true in the strong sense, or more exactly, exhaustive and all-embracing.
And insofar as Phenomenology itself has a philosophical character, it must do the same with its own descriptions.
Admittedly, its descriptions cannot be called fully exhaustive, since Phenomenology describes not the most concrete reality itself but only its appearances, its phenomenological aspect.
But within that aspect, its descriptions must be just as exact, exhaustive, and complete as a philosophical description of reality itself.
Phenomenology must therefore itself demonstrate both this exactness and completeness and the fact that its description of phenomena must be supplemented by a description of the reality that appears.
Only by doing this can it become what it is above all meant to be: a dialectical introduction to philosophy.

Once it has described all phenomena exactly and exhaustively, it shows, first, why the philosophical question in the strict sense must be asked—the question of the “cause” of those phenomena. And second, it gives the philosopher the means to answer that question exhaustively.

How, then—by what “method”—can Phenomenology show, on the one hand, that its descriptions are exact and exhaustive and, on the other, prove that the work itself is genuinely complete, that it describes all phenomena?
We know that, for Hegel, philosophy can prove its own truth only because, in being true, it is also circular.
And we already know what this circularity means: philosophy returns to its point of departure and repeats what it has already passed through.
In principle, philosophical “circularity” can begin anywhere.

What matters is that, after beginning with the description of some particular appearance—or some “element,” “moment,” or “stage” of reality—philosophy must pass necessarily and universally to the description of another.
And this other element is precisely determined. From A, one must necessarily and universally pass to B; one cannot pass directly to C, D, E, and so on, at least not without first passing through B.
By moving from one description to another in this way, philosophy finally returns to the description with which it began.
If we wish to continue, all we can do is trace the same circle again, indefinitely. Having gone from Z to A, we must once again go from A to B, then from B to C, and so on until Z; then begin again.
